title: SGH opens new emergency and neuroscience building, cuts stroke treatment time to 82 minutes
text: SGH opens new emergency and neuroscience building, cuts stroke treatment time to 82 minutes Singapore General Hospital's new 12-storey Emergency and National Neuroscience Institute building reduces acute stroke treatment time from 130 to 82 minutes and is six times larger than its previous space. Patients suffering from acute strokes can now be assessed, scanned, and treated in as quickly as 82 minutes at the newly opened Singapore General Hospital (SGH) Emergency and National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) building. This is down from 130 minutes previously, as the new facility co-locates emergency care and neuroscience intervention to speed diagnosis and treatment. The 12-storey facility, spanning 14,000 sq m, is six times larger than its previous space in Block 1. It was officially opened by Minister for Health Ong Ye Kung on Oct 30. The building is designed to manage heavy patient volumes and complex medical crises while eliminating potentially severe hospital transit delays.Purpose built stroke response centreIt is purpose-built to consolidate emergency assessment, acute medical care and advanced neuroscience intervention into one space, as part of the ongoing transformation of the SGH campus in Outram. Ong said the co-location with NNI is by design, to provide a faster response to stroke patients, as a blocked blood vessel needs to be cleared within the golden hour.Locating Singapore first emergency department-based angiography suite at the ED allows patients to undergo endovascular thrombectomy, a life-saving intervention to reopen blocked blood vessels in the brain, within minutes of diagnosis without transfer to the SGH main blocks. When it comes to stroke treatment, time is brain. Every minute a blood vessel remains blocked, millions of brain cells die. Longer transit times increase the risk of permanent brain damage, severe disability and poorer long-term survival rates.The ED continues to be the front line of a healthcare institution and the bridge between what is happening inside the hospital and the outside environment, Ong said. If bed occupancy shoots up in the hospital wards and admissions slow down, the bottleneck is immediately felt in the ED. By looking at the ED, we can immediately gauge the health status of the community and the hospital.Expanded emergency department facilitiesThe new SGH emergency department has 10 triage rooms, up from four in the old Block 1 facility. The ED comprises 53 critical care area cubicles over two floors and 12 resuscitation rooms. The building also houses acute medical wards with over 150 short-stay beds, neuroscience specialist outpatient clinics, and advanced imaging including MRI and interventional radiology.One of the two critical care areas, with 29 cubicles, can be converted into a negative pressure area in case of a pandemic, said Dr Ivan Chua, head and senior consultant at the SGH department of Emergency Medicine. Ong said that shortly after joining MOH, he learnt that the measure of whether an ED is running at full capacity is not whether the ambulance bays are filled, but whether the resuscitation rooms are filled.Managing patient wait times and expectationsOn an average day, the SGH ED sees over 300 patients, and typically about 15 per cent need immediate attention and are given priority. When people tell him they waited a few hours at the ED, Ong tells them it is a good thing because it means their conditions are not serious. He hopes more people can appreciate that unique operational environment of an ED and sought understanding when longer waits are necessary.With the new ED, spaces, workflows and teams have been brought together around the patient, said SGH CEO Tan Hiang Khoon. Managing pressure also means recognising that not everyone who comes to the ED requires emergency care, Ong said. With telehealth platforms and GPs providing alternative care, wait times over the last three years for 95 per cent of serious but not life-threatening emergency cases at SGH have fallen from 217 minutes in 2023 to 141 minutes in 2025.
